newsitem.title: AUSTRALIA: Australian wages jump rules out rate cut.
newsitem.headline: Australian wages jump rules out rate cut.

text.p: Australian economists received a rude shock on Thursday when key wages data came in above even the most pessimistic forecasts, a figure that was seen ruling out virtually any possibility of a near-term interest rate cut.

Official data showed that average weekly ordinary time earnings (AWOTE) rose 1.3 percent in the three months to February, well above median forecasts of a 0.8 percent rise and the largest quarterly rise since May 1995.
"Today's earnings data represent the first grey cloud in the otherwise clear skies of the inflation outlook," Commonwealth Bank senior economist Michael Blythe said.

The quarterly jump took annual wages growth to 4.6 percent. Not only was it the highest annual rate in over one year, but it also took AWOTE above the 4.5 percent pace seen as the Reserve Bank of Australia's (RBA) "line in the sand" on wages growth.
Beyond 4.5 percent wages are seen posing a threat to low inflation and damaging the case for another rate cut.
"Any small likelihood of a rate cut from next Tuesday's RBA board meeting has now vanished," HSBC Markets chief economist John Edwards said.
Apart from the possible implications for inflation, analysts also expressed some concern at the pace of wages growth given the unemployment rate had stalled above 8.5 percent.
"It must be a real concern to policy makers that we are getting such wage outcomes when the labour market is so weak," Citibank Australia chief economist Stephen Koukoulas said.

Building approvals data for March was also released on Thursday, and while the fall of 1.8 percent was slightly disappointing, economists said the underlying tone was consistent with continued housing improvement through 1997.
Importantly, private sector housing approvals rose 4.1 percent in the month, and once monthly volatility was substracted the postive tone became more apparent.
In the March quarter, average monthly approvals were 5.3 higher than in the December quarter and 14.1 percent higher than in the March quarter last year.
"The data does conform to a picture of a housing sector on the rise, and this should be a positive for the economy as the year progresses," Bankers Trust senior economist Peter Munckton said.

With that outlook, and the preliminary signs of stronger wages, the odds on a rate cut had lengthened, but economists said there was also no need for a rate hike -- instead official rates were seen as likely to remain at 6.0 percent until 1998.
There were also some doubts over the wages numbers, with economists wanting to see data due later this month which will show the pace of AWOTE in the public and private sectors.
If government cut backs had affected lower paid public sector workers, it would lift public sector AWOTE above the rate of rises actually being paid, which appeared to have occured.

The latest available data shows that in the year to November, public sector AWOTE rose 7.6 percent while private sector AWOTE, which is seen as a better indicator of inflation pressure, was running at 2.8 percent.
But whatever the doubts over the data, economists said it highly unlikely that the RBA would consider a rate cut just now.
"Basically forget any prospect of another cut in interest rates until it becomes clear that this is not a sign of accelerating wages growth," Dresdner chief economist Rob Henderson said.
